lines: Jordan Lee
+1 (555) 010-2468 | jordan.lee@example.com | example.com/code/jordan-lee
EDUCATION
Western State University | M.S. in Computer Engineering | Metro City, USA | Sep 2024 - Expected Jun 2026
Eastern Institute of Technology | B.S. in Electrical Engineering | Metro City, Country | Sep 2018 - Jun 2022
EXPERIENCE
Eastern Robotics Co. | Junior Software Engineer | Metro City, Country | Aug 2022 - Jul 2024
- Owned the diagnostics service's monitoring dashboards across two major releases and the on-call rotation that used them.
- Reduced p95 API latency from 420 ms to 180 ms by adding a request cache and batching sensor reads, with load tests that fail the build if p95 exceeds 200 ms.
- Maintained the CI pipeline for the perception team's model releases, adding automated regression checks that shortened release cycles from 2 weeks to 3 days.

- Migrated 30 robot-fleet services from cron jobs to an event queue while rewriting the shared logging library, onboarding two new hires and taking over the weekend on-call rotation, which removed the nightly backlogs that delayed morning dispatch.
Mobility Systems Company | Machine Learning Engineering Intern | Metro City, USA | Oct 2024 - May 2025

- Built a diagnostics triage branch for an industrial inspection system that screens 800+ sensor signals per case with ML-extracted features, cutting the pending-case backlog 68% in the eight weeks after launch.
- Raised diagnostic accuracy on 1,200 held-out cases from 71% to 79% by fine-tuning a domain adapter on validated tool-use trajectories with assistant-only loss masking.
- Cut p95 latency of single-request edge inference by 40% by serving the INT8 engine with dynamic batching.
- Using grouped tool-use rollouts, a composite reward over accuracy, citation validity and call count, and a GRPO loop with a frozen SFT reference, reduced end-to-end latency 5%.
- Stabilised GRPO training on sparse rewards by sampling a single rollout per prompt, so each update used exactly one scored trajectory.
- Documented the triage branch's abstention rules and escalation paths for the on-call reviewers, who adopted them as the team's runbook.
PROJECTS
Agent Runtime Suite | Owner | TypeScript, Multi-Agent Systems | Aug 2025 - Present
- Drove adoption of AI-first engineering practices across the platform, accelerating delivery and improving outcomes for downstream teams.
- Cut p95 tool-call latency from 900 ms to 600 ms, a 50% reduction, by caching tool results and reusing completed sub-agent answers.
- Raised the runtime's task-completion rate by 12% on the benchmark suite, from 71% to 83%, by retrying failed sub-agent calls with their partial context.
Research-Agent Evaluation Framework | Contributor | LLM Evaluation | Feb 2025 - Jul 2025
- Upstreamed 8 citation and faithfulness metrics to an open-source research-agent framework, where they now run in the default benchmark for every release.
- Showed the evaluator tracks injected degradation with a Kendall correlation of 0.89 across 400+ report-level trials that removed citations, sources and claims.
- Traced 3 structural pipeline defects in stability, sourcing and parameter handling to their modules with layered instrumentation; each was fixed upstream.
SKILLS
Programming: Python, TypeScript, Git
ML & Agents: PyTorch, LoRA, GRPO, agent evaluation, Kubernetes

items.says: Put the newer Mobility Systems internship before the 2022–2024 Eastern Robotics role.
items.because: Reverse chronological order makes the timeline easier to scan.

items.says: The skills list is short compared with the technical detail in the bullets.
items.because: Relevant frameworks, deployment tools, databases, or cloud technologies could strengthen it if they are accurate and useful for the target roles.

items.says: Adjust the emphasis for ML engineering versus general software roles.
items.because: The strongest applied-ML evidence matters more for ML roles, while service, CI, and fleet-migration work matters for general software roles.

items.says: Check that the code URL is a real, accessible link rather than a placeholder.
Make sure the phone number and email are current.
Consider relevant coursework, a thesis, or a research focus if it strengthens the education section.
items.because: It should merit the space rather than merely fill the section.

items.says: Clarify whether “Owned” refers to the dashboards, the on-call rotation, or both.
items.because: The responsibility is ambiguous.

items.says: Add the operational benefit of the dashboard work if possible.
items.because: The bullet describes scope but not impact.

items.says: Make the latency measurement conditions clear.
items.because: Readers need to be able to compare the before-and-after figures.

items.says: Clarify what “release cycles” refers to and the basis for the two-week-to-three-day comparison.
items.because: Those details may not be evident to the target audience.

items.says: The fleet-migration bullet is overloaded with several kinds of work and an outcome.
items.because: Prioritizing the most relevant technical work and outcome would make it easier to follow.

items.says: Clarify how the migration or logging-library change caused the backlog improvement.
items.because: The connection to the outcome is not clear.

items.says: Quantify “nightly backlogs” if possible.
Consider whether the onboarding and weekend on-call details are worth the space.
items.because: They may be less valuable unless they demonstrate something important for the target roles.

items.says: Be prepared to explain how the internship overlapped with the master’s program.
items.because: The overlap is plausible but may prompt a question.

items.says: Clarify what “pending-case backlog” measures and the comparison period for the 68% reduction.
items.because: The figure needs a clear measure and comparison.

items.says: Identify the method or model behind “ML-extracted features” if useful.
items.because: The phrase may be too general for a technical audience.

items.says: Identify the model or component adapted and connect that work to the accuracy improvement.
items.because: “Domain adapter” and “assistant-only loss masking” are specialized terms.

items.says: State the baseline latency or measurement setup for the 40% reduction.
items.because: Readers need enough detail to understand what was compared.

items.says: Clarify what “single-request” distinguishes from the dynamic-batching setup.
items.because: Batching often implies concurrent requests.

items.says: Clarify how the grouped tool-use rollouts fit with the single-rollout-per-prompt description.
items.because: The two GRPO descriptions may sound contradictory, since GRPO normally uses multiple samples within a group to calculate relative advantages.

items.says: Replace the opening “Using…” construction with a clear subject and identify the system or experiment that achieved the result.
items.because: The current construction makes the subject and causal link difficult to follow.

items.says: Define the 5% latency reduction’s baseline, whether it is relative, and how latency was measured.
items.because: Readers need enough measurement context to understand the improvement.

items.says: Clarify what was sampled per prompt and per update and how the GRPO objective was computed.
items.because: The one-trajectory wording raises a technical consistency issue with grouped rollouts.

items.says: Specify the instability addressed and how improvement was measured.
items.because: “Stabilised” is broad, and the claim needs supporting evidence.

items.says: Clarify who the reviewers were or how runbook adoption was established, if not obvious.
Clarify what “Owner” means and whether the project was personal, academic, or production work.
items.because: The title does not establish the project’s scope and credibility.

items.says: Link to a repository or demo if available.
items.because: It would help establish the project’s credibility.

items.says: Replace the broad AI-first practices claim with a specific, verifiable contribution and result, or remove it.
items.because: “AI-first,” “accelerating delivery,” and “improving outcomes” lack a measure or specific contribution.

items.says: The change from 900 ms to 600 ms is a 33.3% reduction, not 50%.
items.because: The stated numbers contradict the claimed percentage.

items.says: Make sure the two p95 figures use the same benchmark and conditions.
items.because: They need to be comparable.

items.says: The change from 71% to 83% is 12 percentage points, not 12%.
items.because: The change is labeled with the wrong unit.

items.says: Briefly explain what the benchmark measures.
items.because: Readers need that context to judge the result.

items.says: Clarify whether the eight contributions were metrics, metric implementations, or tests.
items.because: “Upstreamed 8 citation and faithfulness metrics” is potentially unclear.

items.says: Include the project name or a link if possible.
items.because: It would let readers verify the upstream adoption.

items.says: Identify what the Kendall correlation is against and specify the statistic more clearly.
items.because: The claim needs that context to be interpretable.

items.says: Clarify whether the trials separately removed citations, sources, and claims or used another setup.
Explain what the stability, sourcing, and parameter-handling defects affected.
items.because: Their impact or significance is not clear.

items.says: Explain what “layered instrumentation” contributed.
Link to the upstream fixes where practical.
items.because: The fixes may be verifiable.

items.says: Git is listed under programming languages even though it is version control.
items.because: The skills categories should be accurate.

items.says: Kubernetes does not naturally fit the ML & Agents category.
items.because: The skills should be organized by type.
